candidates.name: Reflexion (Shinn et al., NeurIPS 2023)
candidates.task_shape: Agent attempts a task (ALFWorld env, HotpotQA, HumanEval-style coding), fails, receives an EXTERNAL binary/scalar signal (env reward or unit-test pass/fail), writes a verbal self-reflection into episodic memory, and retries — repeated up to ~10 trials for coding tasks.
candidates.grading: External ground-truth signal per trial (env reward / unit test pass-fail), not LLM-judge or human.
candidates.official_protocol: No single official harness; per-task loops (ALFWorld env steps, HumanEval unit tests). Multiple trials per task, each trial = 1 full model rollout + 1 reflection call. NOT budget-matched to baseline out of the box: N trials vs 1 for vanilla agent — flagged directly by Kamoi et al. 2024's critique of this class of paper.
candidates.size_and_versions: 3 task families used across HumanEval/MBPP-style coding, HotpotQA, ALFWorld; no single fixed 'current version' — paper is 2023, no known deprecation.
candidates.requirements: None beyond an environment with a reliable pass/fail or reward signal per trial; no GPU/docker needed for the concept, only for the target task env.
candidates.supported_agents: N/A — this is a prompting/memory technique, not a fixed harness; not natively wired into pi/OpenCode/Claude Code/Codex.
candidates.small_open_model_results: Not tested on small open-weight models in the original paper (GPT-3.5/GPT-4 era); no <=35B numbers found in this pass — unverified for our model regime.
candidates.fit: Relevant as the origin of 'external signal + verbal reflection + retry' pattern that Vacant's Arm C generalizes (trace evidence = the external signal), but its per-trial cost (multiple full rollouts) doesn't fit our zero-config/cheap-redo goal directly; more useful as citation than as protocol to copy.
candidates.cost_time: Paper's own accounting: up to ~10 full trials per task in coding settings; no per-token cost reported (pre-dates today's metered APIs). Under our 50 free-calls/day cap, a Reflexion-style multi-trial loop would consume most of the daily budget on a handful of tasks.
candidates.risks: Budget confound (N trials vs 1) explicitly flagged by Kamoi et al.; quality depends entirely on the external signal being trustworthy — degrades if the only 'signal' is the model's own success judgment.

candidates.name: Self-Refine (Madaan et al., NeurIPS 2023)
candidates.task_shape: Single LLM plays generator+critic+refiner on 7 tasks (dialogue response, code optimization, math reasoning, acronym generation, sentiment reversal, constrained generation, code readability/PIE). Iterates until the model's own feedback says 'good' or a max-iteration cap.
candidates.grading: Mix of automatic metrics (task-specific, e.g. exact match for math, PIE readability score) and human/LLM preference judgments for open-ended tasks.
candidates.official_protocol: No external verifier — pure intrinsic self-critique loop, no tools. Kamoi et al. 2024 identifies this paper by name as methodologically UNFAIR: the initial generation is given a weaker prompt/fewer few-shot examples than the refinement step gets, inflating the apparent gain.
candidates.size_and_versions: 7 benchmark tasks, standard splits per task (paper 2023); no updated/'v2' harness known.
candidates.requirements: None beyond API access to the target LLM; no external tools or ground truth used.
candidates.supported_agents: N/A — prompting technique, not an agent harness.
candidates.small_open_model_results: Original paper tested GPT-3.5/ChatGPT/GPT-4 class only; no <=35B open-weight numbers found in this pass — unverified for small models.
candidates.fit: Directly the structure of our Arm B (reviewer persona, no external evidence) MINUS the asymmetric-prompt flaw Kamoi et al. found — we must NOT replicate that flaw (keep Arm A's and Arm B's initial-pass prompt identical) or we reproduce exactly the bias this survey calls out.
candidates.cost_time: Iterative loop, cost scales with max-iteration cap (paper used small caps, typically <=4); token cost modest per task but not separately reported in $ terms (pre-dates today's metered pricing).
candidates.risks: Confirmed by Kamoi et al. as an example of unfair evaluation (asymmetric prompt strength between initial and refine passes); intrinsic-only feedback has no external grounding, so per Huang et al./#10 below it risks making correct answers worse on reasoning-style tasks.

candidates.name: CRITIC (Gou et al., ICLR 2024)
candidates.task_shape: LLM generates an initial output, then iteratively critiques+corrects it using EXTERNAL TOOLS (web search for QA, code interpreter for math, Perspective API for toxicity) as the verification signal, rather than pure self-talk.
candidates.grading: Automatic: EM/F1 for QA (AmbigNQ, TriviaQA, HotpotQA, 500 samples each), exact match for math (GSM8K, SVAMP, TabMWP official test splits), Perspective-API toxicity score for RealToxicityPrompts (1k prompts).
candidates.official_protocol: Exact and reusable: QA = max 3 correction rounds, up to 7 tool calls/round, early-stop if answer unchanged 2 rounds running; math = max 4 rounds, early-stop on unchanged execution result x2; toxicity = max 4 iterations, stop when toxicity <10%. Baselines at matched/larger budget: rejection sampling (N fresh generations), self-consistency voting, and an explicitly-labeled oracle upper bound (CRITIC*, corrects only known-wrong samples).
candidates.size_and_versions: Models: text-davinci-003, ChatGPT(gpt-3.5-turbo), LLaMA-2 7B/13B/70B. Benchmarks as above, standard test splits, 2023-24 vintage, still current (no successor version known).
candidates.requirements: Needs a real web-search tool and a code interpreter/sandbox for full effect; a 'w/o tool' ablation condition exists and is directly informative for us.
candidates.supported_agents: N/A — a prompting+tool-use loop, portable to any agent harness in principle, not tied to a specific one.
candidates.small_open_model_results: LLaMA-2 7B on TabMWP: CRITIC (tool-grounded) +4.7pp over baseline; 13B +9.4pp; 70B +16.0pp — gains scale UP with size, so smallest open model in this range gets the smallest absolute lift from the same tool-grounded loop.
candidates.fit: THE key empirical anchor for our A/B/C design: CRITIC w/o tool ~= our Arm B (near-zero or slightly negative F1 change, -0.03 to +2.33 on QA); full tool-grounded CRITIC ~= our Arm C. Confirms the B-vs-C gap direction but warns it will likely be smaller at 9-12B than at GPT-3.5/70B scale.
candidates.cost_time: Per task: up to 3-4 model calls for the base loop plus up to 7 tool calls per round (tool calls typically far cheaper than model calls, but still add latency); directly reusable call-budget bookkeeping style for our own accounting.
candidates.risks: Explicitly states intrinsic self-correction ('w/o tool') 'may yield modest improvements or even deteriorate performance' — this is a load-bearing citation for treating Arm B underperforming Arm A as an expected, reportable finding rather than a bug.

candidates.name: Huang et al., LLMs Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
candidates.task_shape: GPT-3.5/GPT-4 answer a reasoning question, are asked to review/find problems with NO external feedback, and revise; also a separate oracle-gated condition (uses ground truth only to decide whether to keep the revision) as an explicitly-labeled upper bound, not a real deployment setting.
candidates.grading: Deterministic exact-match accuracy per benchmark (GSM8K, CommonSenseQA, HotpotQA); also a flip-direction analysis (correct->wrong vs wrong->correct after correction).
candidates.official_protocol: Explicit call-budget bookkeeping we can copy directly: standard prompting = 1 call; round-1 self-correction = 3 calls (generate/critique/revise); round-2 = 5 calls total. Max 2 rounds. Oracle condition clearly separated from the 'intrinsic, no oracle' condition that is the paper's real result.
candidates.size_and_versions: GSM8K, CommonSenseQA, HotpotQA, standard test splits, GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4 (2023-24); benchmarks still standard/current.
candidates.requirements: None beyond API access; no tools, no ground truth used in the real (intrinsic) condition.
candidates.supported_agents: N/A — single-turn reasoning QA/math setting, not a coding-agent harness.
candidates.small_open_model_results: Not tested on small open models (GPT-3.5/4 only) — unverified for our <=35B regime, though directionally corroborated at small scale by candidate #10 below.
candidates.fit: Canonical citation for why Arm B is a necessary control and may legitimately underperform Arm A; also shows multi-agent debate (6 agents, 83.2%) scored BELOW plain self-consistency (85.3%) at the same call budget — argues for keeping our Arm B simple/cheap rather than elaborating it into multi-persona debate.
candidates.cost_time: Exact numbers from the paper: 1 call (baseline) vs 3 calls (round 1) vs 5 calls (round 2) per task — directly reusable template for our own per-arm call/token/cost reporting.
candidates.risks: Central, quantified pitfall: on GSM8K, GPT-3.5-class model kept its original answer 74.7% of the time under self-correction and introduced NEW errors in most of the remaining cases — 'more likely to break a correct answer than fix a wrong one.' CommonSenseQA collapsed 75.8%->38.1%->41.8% under intrinsic self-correction.

candidates.name: Tyen et al., LLMs cannot find reasoning errors but can correct given the error location (ACL Findings 2024) / BIG-Bench Mistake
candidates.task_shape: Model produces a CoT trace on one of 5 tasks (word sorting, tracking shuffled objects, logical deduction, multistep arithmetic, Dyck languages); mistake-step is located under 3 conditions (oracle/human-annotated, random control, model/classifier-found); the erroneous step is regenerated at temp=1 (up to 8 resamples) then all subsequent steps regenerated at temp=0.
candidates.grading: Deterministic: accuracy on final answer after correction, split by originally-correct vs originally-incorrect traces; separately, mistake-LOCATION accuracy of the model/classifier vs the human-annotated ground truth (Krippendorff's alpha 0.979-0.998, i.e. ground truth is highly reliable).
candidates.official_protocol: 2186 CoT traces total: 4 tasks x 300 traces each (~85% incorrect/15% correct by design) + 986 Dyck-language traces. Oracle-vs-random-vs-model-found location is the core ablation — this IS the fair-comparison structure (isolates 'does knowing the location help' from 'does resampling help at all').
candidates.size_and_versions: BIG-Bench Mistake dataset, released with this paper (2023-24), 2186 traces; no newer version found in this pass.
candidates.requirements: None beyond the released dataset (public) and API access to the model being corrected/located.
candidates.supported_agents: N/A — single-turn CoT correction, not an agent-tool harness.
candidates.small_open_model_results: A small trained classifier ('Unicorn'/PaLM-2 Otter, out-of-domain trained) beat prompted mistake-finding on 4/5 tasks but only reached 6.00%-37.67% absolute location accuracy, below the ~60-70% the authors estimate is needed for reliable backtracking payoff — a caution about relying on a small model to FIND errors unaided.
candidates.fit: THE single most load-bearing paper for Vacant's core design bet: oracle-location correction gave +18.04pp to +43.92pp on originally-wrong traces (vs much smaller gains under random location), directly justifying Vacant's file:line:step-located feedback (Arm C) over ask-the-model-to-find-its-own-error (Arm B, shown separately in this paper to be weak).
candidates.cost_time: Per trace: 1 generation call + up to 8 resample calls for the erroneous step + forward regeneration of subsequent steps; no seeds/multi-trial reporting found in the extracted text (unverified whether repeated trials were run — flag if statistical power matters).
candidates.risks: Headline finding itself IS the risk to internalize: models are bad at finding their own errors (motivating Arm B's expected weakness) even though they are good at fixing errors once located (motivating Arm C); no seed/trial-count info found, so effect-size precision is somewhat unverified.

candidates.name: Kamoi et al., When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey (TACL 2024, vol 12)
candidates.task_shape: Not an experiment itself — a meta-survey defining a taxonomy (intrinsic vs external-feedback; fair/unfair/unrealistic evaluation) and auditing prior self-correction papers against it, naming specific methodological flaws (oracle leakage, asymmetric prompt strength, inconsistent resource allocation) in named papers including Self-Refine and RCI Prompting.
candidates.grading: N/A (survey); provides a checklist (their Tables 7-8) for designing/reporting a fair self-correction comparison.
candidates.official_protocol: Their prescribed checklist, directly reusable for our arm design: (1) state exact research question + which taxonomy category the experiment is; (2) no oracle information anywhere in the loop including whether to run correction; (3) use the SAME strong prompt for the initial pass regardless of condition; (4) compare against self-consistency/generate-and-rerank as an equal-extra-compute baseline, not just vs 1-shot; (5) if resources genuinely differ between conditions, say so explicitly rather than calling the comparison 'fair.'
candidates.size_and_versions: Survey covering dozens of papers through mid-2024; TACL 2024 vol.12 pp.1417-1440; no dataset/benchmark of its own.
candidates.requirements: None — literature synthesis only.
candidates.supported_agents: N/A.
candidates.small_open_model_results: N/A (survey, not new experiments); notes fine-tuned-feedback approaches typically needed 100K+ training instances, ruling those out as zero-config options for us.
candidates.fit: This is the paper to write our methods section against. Its central conclusion for us: our A/B/C comparison should be framed explicitly as an EVIDENCE ABLATION (does having Vacant's grounded trace change the outcome) rather than claimed as a strict resource-matched self-correction ablation, since Arm A/B structurally cannot have Vacant's evidence — state that plainly per their transparency requirement rather than overclaim 'fairness.'
candidates.cost_time: N/A directly, but the checklist implies we must report calls/tokens/cost per arm with the same rigor as Huang et al.'s 1/3/5-call accounting, or our comparison will be exactly the kind of unfair setup this survey names and critiques.
candidates.risks: Its own risk-list IS the deliverable: oracle leakage (e.g. deciding whether to run correction using the answer), asymmetric initial-prompt strength (Self-Refine's flaw — do not replicate in our Arm A vs B), and uncredited extra tool/resource access during refinement only (do not give Arm C tools during redo that Arm A/B could have used during the first pass, if those tools are not Vacant-specific evidence).

candidates.name: Agent-as-a-Judge (Zhuge et al., 2024)
candidates.task_shape: An agentic judge (which can itself act — inspect files, read intermediate trajectory artifacts, not just the final output) evaluates another agent's completed run, on 3 existing agentic coding systems, compared against plain LLM-as-a-Judge (final-output-only) and human evaluators.
candidates.grading: Agreement/correlation with human evaluation as the ground truth for judge quality; reported as close to human-eval reliability and clearly ahead of output-only LLM-as-a-Judge.
candidates.official_protocol: Not fully extracted in this pass — exact model-call budget vs the LLM-as-a-Judge baseline was not found in available snippets; UNVERIFIED, would need direct PDF read if this number is needed for our writeup.
candidates.size_and_versions: 3 pre-existing agentic coding systems as the evaluation targets (2024 vintage); specific benchmark/version numbers not confirmed in this pass.
candidates.requirements: Needs the target agent's full intermediate trajectory/artifacts available to the judge, not just final output — structurally the same evidence-availability requirement Vacant's trace layer satisfies.
candidates.supported_agents: N/A — a judge methodology, not itself an installable agent harness.
candidates.small_open_model_results: Not found in this pass — unverified whether small open-weight models were tested as the judge.
candidates.fit: Closest prior work to our reviewer-persona step: shows a TRAJECTORY-GROUNDED judge beats an output-only judge, which is structurally the same claim as 'Arm C (evidence-grounded) beats Arm B (ungrounded persona)' — good supporting citation, though it evaluates judge quality rather than measuring downstream task-improvement from sending work back for redo.
candidates.cost_time: Unverified this pass (see official_protocol) — flag as needing a follow-up read if exact numbers matter.
candidates.risks: Main caveat is our own uncertainty about its exact protocol details (unverified budget), not a reported failure mode of the method itself in the snippets we could pull.

candidates.name: OpenHands verification stack / critic model (industry blog, 2025-2026, not peer-reviewed)
candidates.task_shape: Two-layer system: (1) an agent-level CRITIC model scores the full agent trajectory (not just final diff) and can trigger 'iterative refinement' — send the agent back with a below-threshold score before the change is proposed; (2) a repo-level verifier reviews the resulting PR in normal code review. Critic is trained on real production traces (supervised), not prompted self-critique.
candidates.grading: Critic outputs a trajectory score against a threshold; blog claims 'high accuracy on predicting outcomes on production data' but does not give the metric/number in the page we read.
candidates.official_protocol: NOT fully extractable from the public blog post read in this pass — exact retry-count/threshold defaults, compute-budget parity vs a no-critic baseline, and critic model size were all deferred to a separate linked post/paper (arxiv.org/abs/2603.03800, not independently re-verified). Their April 2025 SWE-bench-Verified SOTA announcement is known only via secondary/search-snippet sources in this pass — UNVERIFIED, treat as unconfirmed until the primary source is read directly.
candidates.size_and_versions: OpenHands platform, 2025-2026 vintage, actively developed (blog dated 2026-06-22 per page timestamp); SWE-bench Verified (500-problem, human-confirmed-solvable subset) is the implied benchmark but not independently re-confirmed for this specific claim.
candidates.requirements: Requires OpenHands platform + a trained critic model (their own, not off-the-shelf) + production trace data to train it — not zero-config, not directly portable to Vacant's rule-based (non-trained) trace/locate approach.
candidates.supported_agents: OpenHands's own agent, not the pi/OpenCode/Claude Code/Codex set we target; architecturally analogous but not directly reusable.
candidates.small_open_model_results: Not found — unverified.
candidates.fit: Reassuring existence proof at industry scale that 'trajectory-grounded critic + localized send-back before delivery' (structurally = Vacant's own architecture) is a viable production pattern, but we cannot cite specific numbers without a follow-up read of the underlying paper.
candidates.cost_time: Not extractable this pass — unverified.
candidates.risks: Primary risk is citation risk: several specific claims (SOTA %, critic size, budget parity) are unverified from this pass and should not be quoted as fact without re-reading arxiv.org/abs/2603.03800 directly.

candidates.name: When Agents go Astray: Course-Correcting SWE Agents with PRMs (Gandhi et al., arXiv 2509.02360, NeurIPS 2025)
candidates.task_shape: An inference-time Process Reward Model watches a coding agent's SWE-bench trajectory DURING execution (step-level, not just at the end) and intervenes on specific trajectory-level inefficiency patterns (redundant exploration, looping, failure to terminate once solved), using a taxonomy of common inefficiencies to generate lightweight interpretable feedback without modifying the underlying policy.
candidates.grading: SWE-bench Verified resolution rate (does the generated patch pass the held-out tests), a fully deterministic pass/fail metric per instance.
candidates.official_protocol: PRM trained on labeled trajectory-level error taxonomy; intervenes inline during a single agent run (course-correction), compared against the same agent without PRM intervention on the same 500-problem SWE-bench Verified set.
candidates.size_and_versions: SWE-bench Verified, 500 human-confirmed-solvable instances (current official subset per OpenAI's 2024 announcement, still standard as of 2026); paper is 2025 (NeurIPS 2025).
candidates.requirements: Needs a trained PRM (its own training data/infra) plus the standard SWE-bench Verified docker-based eval harness (per-instance repo checkout + test execution) — meaningful compute/disk requirement, not zero-config.
candidates.supported_agents: Not tied to a specific one of our 4 target agents; demonstrated on their own SWE-bench agent scaffold.
candidates.small_open_model_results: Reported closed-source PRM numbers only (40.0%->50.6%, +10.6pp); no <=35B open-model PRM numbers found in this pass — unverified for our regime.
candidates.fit: Strongest available large-scale NUMERIC anchor that external, step-level (not just outcome-level) verification measurably improves coding-agent outcomes on a fully deterministic benchmark; gains concentrated on medium/hard tasks (not uniform) — matches our expectation that Vacant's lift should show up most where evidence genuinely disambiguates something, not on tasks the agent would nail anyway.
candidates.cost_time: Not fully itemized in calls/tokens in the snippets read; the deterministic SWE-bench harness itself is compute-heavy (full repo checkout + test suite per instance) — a caution if we ever wanted to run actual SWE-bench Verified ourselves under our $5/50-calls-per-day constraint (almost certainly infeasible at scale; would need a tiny subset).
candidates.risks: Requires trained-model infrastructure (PRM), a different mechanism from Vacant's rule-based, zero-training trace/locate — same causal claim (localized signal beats none) but not a directly portable technique; gains non-uniform across difficulty, so citing the headline +10.6pp without the difficulty breakdown would overstate generality.

candidates.name: When Small Models Are Right for Wrong Reasons: Process Verification for Trustworthy Agents (arXiv 2601.00513, 2026 preprint)
candidates.task_shape: Evaluates 7-9B open models (Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, Qwen-2.5-7B) at greedy decoding (temp=0) on fact-grounded and reasoning tasks, comparing self-critique/verification WITHOUT external grounding vs RAG WITH (oracle) external grounding, and separately measuring whether CORRECT final answers were reached via sound reasoning (a 'Reasoning Integrity Score').
candidates.grading: Reasoning Integrity Score (process-level, not just outcome accuracy) plus Cohen's d effect sizes comparing intervention vs no-intervention conditions; a distilled verifier's detection quality measured by F1.
candidates.official_protocol: Consistent greedy decoding (temp=0) across conditions for comparability; explicitly flags its own RAG condition as using ORACLE retrieval, i.e. an upper bound / potential leakage, and says so openly rather than hiding it — a model of the transparency Kamoi et al. asks for.
candidates.size_and_versions: 7-9B parameter range only (Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, Qwen-2.5-7B); no larger models in the primary analysis; 2026 preprint, arXiv id implies a Jan-2026-era submission.
candidates.requirements: Needs the 3 named 7-9B open-weight models (all obtainable) plus a RAG/retrieval setup for the grounding condition (they used oracle retrieval, i.e. simplified/idealized, not a real retriever) — modest requirements, no docker/GPU specifics given.
candidates.supported_agents: N/A — not an installable agent harness, a controlled model-behavior study.
candidates.small_open_model_results: DIRECTLY on-point for our regime: 50-69% of CORRECT final answers from these 7-9B models involved fundamentally flawed reasoning ('right for wrong reasons'); self-critique/verification WITHOUT grounding: Cohen's d = -0.14 to -0.33 (HARMFUL); external grounding (RAG) on fact-grounded tasks: d = +0.23 to +0.93 (positive, sometimes large). Named failure mode 'pseudo-reflection': small models produce surface-form critique without genuine introspection, and can invent incorrect justifications.
candidates.fit: The single most size-matched piece of evidence we have: at our target ~9-12B scale, ungrounded self-critique (our Arm B) is measured to actively HURT (negative Cohen's d), while external grounding (structurally = our Arm C) helps — a strong, size-appropriate justification for expecting Arm C > Arm A > Arm B is possible, and for reporting Arm B's underperformance as a real, citable, expected finding rather than tuning it away.
candidates.cost_time: Not reported in $/tokens (a model-behavior study, not a cost study); their distilled verifier reached F1 0.86 but only under oracle context (same leakage caveat as their RAG condition) — not a zero-config claim we can port directly.
candidates.risks: 'Pseudo-reflection' is the key named risk: at ~7-12B scale, expect Arm B's critique text to look plausible/confident while not actually re-examining anything, and to sometimes invent wrong justifications that flip a correct judgment to incorrect — worth a manual/LLM-judge spot-check of whether Arm B's critique references anything concrete, if budget allows.

candidates.name: HaluAgent / Small Agent Can Also Rock! (Cheng et al., EMNLP 2024)
candidates.task_shape: A 7B model (Baichuan2-Chat-7B), fine-tuned on ~2K examples, given a multi-functional TOOLBOX (not pure prompting) and a 3-stage detect-locate-verify pipeline with memory, to detect hallucinations in text/code/math outputs, evaluated in-domain and out-of-domain.
candidates.grading: Standard hallucination-detection benchmark metrics (detection accuracy/F1 per dataset, both in-domain and out-of-domain splits); compared against GPT-4 without tool-enhancement as the reference point.
candidates.official_protocol: Fine-tune small base model on ~2K curated examples, then run the 3-stage (detect/locate/verify) tool-using pipeline with memory at inference; compared against zero-shot prompting baselines and GPT-4-without-tools.
candidates.size_and_versions: Baichuan2-Chat-7B base, 2K fine-tuning examples, EMNLP 2024; code/dataset public on GitHub (RUCAIBox/HaluAgent).
candidates.requirements: Needs fine-tuning infrastructure (2K-example SFT run) plus the toolbox implementation — NOT zero-shot/zero-config, a real training step is required, unlike Vacant's rule-based trace/locate.
candidates.supported_agents: N/A — a hallucination-detector model/pipeline, not one of our 4 target coding-agent harnesses.
candidates.small_open_model_results: Reports 7B HaluAgent (structured, tool-using) performing comparable to or exceeding GPT-4-without-tools on both in-domain and out-of-domain hallucination detection — a concrete existence proof that small models CAN do useful verification work when given tools/structure, contrasting with pure unstructured self-critique failures elsewhere in this set.
candidates.fit: Reinforces the cross-cutting pattern (small models fail at unstructured self-critique, succeed at structured tool-grounded verification): supports designing Arm C's evidence delivery as structured (file:line:step, categorized findings) rather than a free-text 'here's what might be wrong' dump, even though we cannot port HaluAgent's technique directly without a fine-tuning step we're not planning to do.
candidates.cost_time: Requires a one-time 2K-example fine-tuning run (cost/time not itemized in $ in available snippets) plus modest per-task toolbox-call overhead at inference — not directly reusable as a zero-config technique for us, cited only as supporting evidence for the structured-beats-unstructured pattern.
candidates.risks: Main limitation for our purposes: needs training data and a fine-tuning step, so it is NOT a zero-config technique we could adopt as-is; useful only as directional evidence, not as a borrowable protocol.

HEADLINE FOR THE LEAD, distilled from all 11 sources: the literature converges hard on one pattern — UNGROUNDED self-critique (ask the model to find/check its own error with no external signal) is repeatedly shown to be weak-to-harmful (Huang et al. ICLR'24: GSM8K 75.9%->74.7% and CommonSenseQA 75.8%->38.1% after 2 rounds of intrinsic self-correction, model more likely to break a correct answer than fix a wrong one; CRITIC's own 'w/o tool' ablation: -0.03 to +2.33 F1, near-zero; and directly size-matched to our target regime, "When Small Models Are Right for Wrong Reasons" (arXiv 2601.00513) measures Cohen's d = -0.14 to -0.33 for ungrounded self-critique at 7-9B scale, naming the failure mode "pseudo-reflection"). GROUNDED/LOCATED feedback is repeatedly shown to work: Tyen et al. (ACL Findings'24, BIG-Bench Mistake) is the cleanest result — oracle mistake-location gives +18 to +44pp correction on wrong traces, while the SAME models are bad at finding their own error location unprompted; the 2601.00513 paper's RAG/grounded condition gets d=+0.23 to +0.93 at the same 7-9B scale; SWE-PRM (arXiv 2509.02360, NeurIPS'25) gets +10.6pp on SWE-bench Verified from step-level, not just outcome-level, external verification. This is strong, size-appropriate support for Vacant's actual bet: Arm C (Vacant's localized trace evidence) should beat Arm B (reviewer persona, no evidence), and Arm B may legitimately underperform Arm A on some tasks — that should be reported as a real, citable, expected finding (per Huang et al. and 2601.00513), not tuned away.

METHODOLOGY WARNING for our own protocol, from Kamoi et al.'s TACL'24 survey (the paper to design against): our A/B/C comparison is NOT a strictly 'fair' resource-matched self-correction ablation in their technical sense, because Arm A/B structurally cannot have Vacant's trace evidence — we should frame it explicitly as an EVIDENCE ABLATION and say so, rather than claim fairness we don't have. Concretely avoid the two flaws they name by title: (1) Self-Refine's asymmetric-prompt flaw — keep Arm A's and Arm B's FIRST-pass prompt byte-identical, only the post-hoc review step differs; (2) oracle leakage — never use ground truth to decide whether/when to run a review pass. Do use Huang et al.'s exact call-counting style (1 vs 3 vs 5 calls) for our own per-arm cost/token/call reporting, since we're on a metered, capped OpenRouter key. Track BOTH directions of flip (fail->pass and pass->fail) for both Arm B and Arm C, not just net accuracy, per Huang et al.'s method. No paper in this set reliably reported multi-seed self-correction numbers, and our own call/cost budget (50 free calls/day, ~$5 cap per MODELS.md) makes multi-seed replication likely infeasible beyond a couple of exemplar tasks — if so, this is consistent with the project's own KS rule 5 ("demo may say 'visible improvement'; 'proven improvement' needs a pre-registered batch run") and should be stated that way rather than oversold.
